subject: gray seal
title: Seals Can Feel Their Own Oxygen Running Out. Humans Can't

scenes.text: Seals can feel something your body is completely blind to.
Gray seals can stay underwater for up to an hour without drowning.
In 2025, scientists changed the air six young seals breathed before five hundred and ten dives.
More oxygen meant longer dives. Less oxygen, shorter dives. Extra carbon dioxide changed nothing.
So seals seem to sense the oxygen in their own blood. Your body can't. It only tracks carbon dioxide.
That burning urge to breathe underwater isn't telling you you're out of air. A seal actually knows.

description:
In a 2025 Science study, University of St Andrews researchers let six juvenile gray seals breathe air with more or less oxygen, or extra carbon dioxide, before diving for fish.
Across 510 dives, dive time rose and fell with oxygen while carbon dioxide had no effect, suggesting seals perceive their blood oxygen, something humans and most mammals cannot do.
How long can you hold your breath?
first_comment: Breathing normal air, the seals' test dives lasted about four minutes on average. In the wild they can go for an hour. What's your breath-hold record?
